articles.title: Time in the world, and the shape of the verb

article_json.also_called: Tense and aspect: where the twelve tenses come from
article_json.one_line: This shows you how the whole verb system fits together, so twelve tenses turn into three times and two switches.
article_json.short_answer: English changes the verb itself for two times only: now and before now. Everything else adds a helping verb. *writes*, *has written*, *will write*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How many tenses does English have, and how do they fit together?

body.text: Time is one thing. The shape of the verb is another
Ask when something happens and you get an answer about the world. Ask what shape the verb takes and you get an answer about English. The two do not always match.
*The ferry leaves at six tomorrow.* The verb sits in its present shape and the event sits in the future. So the shape of the verb is a choice you make, not a clock you read.

body.gloss: the form of a verb that shows when

show_first.text: The Ashfield clinic opens at eight.
The Ashfield clinic opened late yesterday.
Two nurses write the notes each evening.

body.name_line: The shape the verb takes there is its **tense**.
body.anchor_line: English changes the verb itself for two of these only: now and before now. Everything further needs a helping verb in front of it.

body.gloss: how the action is spread out in time

show_first.text: The crew paints the railings each spring.
The crew is painting the railings today.
The crew has painted the railings already.

body.name_line: What changes across those three is the **aspect**.
body.anchor_line: The time is the same in all three. What moves is how much of the event you are showing the reader.

body.text: Two switches sit on top of the time you pick

body.lead_in: Whatever time you are talking about, two switches are available:
items: *have* plus the third form links the event back from a later point
*be* plus the *-ing* form shows the event in the middle of happening

body.gloss: the plain form: no *be + -ing*, no *have* + third form

show_first.text: The council funds two youth centres.
The council funded two youth centres.
The council will fund two youth centres.

body.name_line: With both switches off, the form is called **simple**.
body.anchor_line: That is the plainest thing you can say about an event. It is a choice you make, not something missing.

body.gloss: the *-ing* form, used for something in the middle of happening

show_first.text: The team is writing the safety report.
The team was writing it all Friday.
The team will be writing it next week.

body.name_line: A form built from *be* and *-ing* is called **continuous**.
body.anchor_line: Nothing in any of those says the job is finished. That is what the *-ing* is doing.

body.gloss: a form that links an earlier time to a later time

show_first.text: The trust has painted every bridge on the line.
The trust had painted it before the inspection.
The trust will have painted it by June.

body.name_line: A form built from *have* and the third form is called **perfect**.
body.anchor_line: Each one stands at a later point and looks back at an earlier one. The two points are what the form is for.

body.text: Why books say English has twelve tenses

Three times, two switches, and every combination gets a name. Three multiplied by four is twelve. The number comes from the layout, so it is a way of showing the system rather than twelve separate things to learn.

body.caption: Three times down the side, two switches across the top.
footnotes: Only two cells change the verb itself: *writes* and *wrote*. Every other cell adds a helping verb.
The same twelve, with how often each one is used, are in [th_tense_grid].

body.lead_in: Only the switches move here. The time stays at now in all four.

items.text: The centre runs a free class on Saturdays.
items.gloss: That is what happens week after week.

items.text: The centre is running a free class this month.
items.gloss: It is on at the moment and it will stop.

items.text: The centre has run the class since March.
items.gloss: It started in March and it is still going.

items.text: The centre has been running the class since March.
items.gloss: The same thing, with the length of time in view.

body.so_what: The time never moved. What moved is how much of the event the reader can see.

body.heard: English has twelve tenses, and you have to learn all twelve before you can write anything.
body.truth: Twelve is the size of the layout, not the size of the job. English changes the verb itself in two places only, now and before now. The other ten forms are those two with a helping verb added.
body.what_to_do: Learn the two switches instead of twelve names. Six of the twelve carry almost all of everyday English, and [th_tense_grid] marks which six.

body.headline: Three times, two switches. That is the whole system.

table.caption: One row per switch setting, at any of the three times.
rows: looking back from a later point
how long it has been going on

articles.title: States, actions, and what a verb needs around it

article_json.also_called: State verbs, transitivity, and verbs that work both ways
article_json.one_line: This tells you why some verbs refuse the *-ing* form, and why some verbs need something after them.
article_json.short_answer: A verb that describes a state, not an action, stays in the plain form. *I know the answer*, never *I am knowing the answer*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Why can I say *I am reading* but not *I am knowing*?

body.text: Some verbs describe a state, and a state has no middle
You can be in the middle of reading, so *I am reading* works. You cannot be in the middle of knowing. You either know a thing or you do not, so English keeps the verb plain.

body.gloss: a verb that describes a state, not an action

show_first.text: Most residents prefer the earlier bus.
The site belongs to the water company.

body.name_line: A verb like that is called a **state verb**.
body.anchor_line: None of those three is something you do. Each one is something that is simply the case, so the continuous form has nothing to show.

body.text: The five families of state verb

body.caption: Five meanings, and the verbs that carry them stay plain.
rows: *like, love, hate, prefer, want, need, wish*
*have, own, belong, contain, include, consist of*
footnotes: This is a list of meanings, not a fixed list of words. The next section shows why.

body.lead_in: Every one of these is about a state, so every verb stays plain.

items.text: The building belongs to the university now.
items.gloss: That is who owns it.

items.text: I need the figures before Thursday.
items.gloss: Without them the work stops.

items.text: The scheme costs the council very little.
items.gloss: It is cheap to run.

items.text: Most drivers know the new route already.
items.gloss: They have learned it and they use it.

body.so_what: Not one of them is an activity you could stop halfway through.

body.text: The same word can name a state or an action
Several of these verbs have two meanings. One is a state and stays plain. The other is something you actually do, and then the continuous is right, because there is a middle to be in.

body.question: Is this something I am doing, or something that is simply the case?

options.label: the state meaning, plain form
options.use_it_when: The verb reports how things are: what you own, what you think, how something strikes you.
options.example: I think the second design is cheaper.

options.label: the action meaning, *-ing* form
options.use_it_when: The verb reports an activity you could stop and start: considering, meeting, tasting, behaving.
options.example: I am thinking about the second design.

a.text: They have two offices in the city.
a.means: Those are the offices the firm owns.

b.text: They are having a meeting in the city.
b.means: The meeting is going on right now.

a.means: She understands what has gone wrong.

b.text: The supervisor is seeing the contractor.

a.means: That is what it is like when you drink it.

b.text: The inspector is tasting the water today.
b.means: She is carrying out a test on it.

a.text: He is careful with the equipment.
a.means: That is what he is like as a worker.

b.text: He is being careful with the equipment.
b.means: He is behaving that way today, and normally he does not.

body.deciding_factor: If you could stop halfway through it, the *-ing* form is available. If you could not, the verb stays plain.
body.trap: You reason that the state is true right now, so the form for right now must be correct. Being true now is not the same as being under way now.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The pair matters most in Speaking Part 1, where *I am wanting* and *I am knowing* are heard in the first minute.

body.text: A state verb takes the plain form. Put it in the *-ing* form only when you have switched to a meaning that names something you do.

body.lead_in: The verb is the same word each time. Only the meaning has switched.

items.text: The panel appears satisfied with the figures.
items.gloss: That is how they come across.

items.text: The author is appearing at the Marlow book fair.
items.gloss: She is going there to speak.

items.text: I feel this is the wrong week for it.
items.gloss: That is my opinion about the timing.

items.text: She is feeling much better since Tuesday.
items.gloss: Her health is improving.

body.so_what: *Appear* and *feel* did not change. What changed is whether they name a state or an activity.

body.text: What a verb needs after it, and what it refuses
A second thing is decided by the verb rather than by you: whether an object can follow it. *Discuss* takes one straight away. *Arrive* takes none at all, so nothing you add can become its object.

body.caption: Three groups, and the third one is where errors come from.
rows: Sales rose. The firm raised prices.
footnotes: The third group is the one to watch. The same verb can name the thing that changes or the person who changes it.

body.lead_in: One verb from the third group, used both ways. Watch what sits in front of it.

items.text: Bus fares increased by a fifth last year.
items.gloss: The fares went up. Nobody is named.

items.text: The operator increased bus fares by a fifth.
items.gloss: The operator did it, and the sentence says so.

items.text: The side door closes at six.
items.gloss: That is what the door does at six.

items.text: The caretaker closes the side door at six.
items.gloss: The caretaker is the one who shuts it.

body.so_what: The verb did not change shape. What changed is whether the sentence names the person behind the change.

body.wrong: I am not understanding the second question.
body.right: I do not understand the second question.
body.why_it_happens: You want to say that the problem is happening right now, and the *-ing* form is the one that means right now. *Understand* names a state, and a state has no middle to be in.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the helping verb and the *-ing*: *I do not understand*.

body.wrong: The committee discussed about the parking plan.
body.right: The committee discussed the parking plan.
body.why_it_happens: *Talk* and *argue* both need *about*, so *discuss* looks as though it should too. *Discuss* takes its object straight, with nothing in between.
body.smallest_fix: Take *about* out. The same goes for *enter*, *answer* and *approach*.

body.wrong: Two serious delays were happened on the Norland line.
body.right: Two serious delays happened on the Norland line.
body.why_it_happens: *Was* plus the third form sounds formal, and formal feels safer in an essay. *Happen* cannot take an object, so there is nobody for that form to hide.
body.smallest_fix: Use the verb on its own: *happened*, *occurred*, *rose*, *fell*.

body.label: Two places where a state verb turns up in the *-ing* form anyway

items.text: *Love*, *like* and *hate* take the *-ing* form in relaxed speech and in advertising.
items.example: I am loving the new cycle lane.

items.text: *Be* takes the *-ing* form when it means behaving that way for the moment.
items.example: The landlord is being difficult about the deposit.

body.heard: *Know*, *want* and *like* can never be used in the *-ing* form.
body.truth: It is not the word that blocks the *-ing* form, it is the meaning. *I am seeing the supervisor at four* is normal English, because *see* there means meet, and meeting is something you do.
body.what_to_do: Ask what the verb means in this sentence rather than checking it against a list. Keep the plain form for a state, and write *I do not understand*, never *I am not understanding*.

body.mechanism: Tamil marks an event as still going on with an ending on the verb, and that ending is available with verbs of knowing and wanting.
body.wrong: I am knowing the timetable.
body.right: I know the timetable.
body.fix: Use the plain form for knowing, wanting and owning, even when you mean right now.

body.headline: No middle, no *-ing*. No object, no doer in front.

table.caption: One row per question you ask about the verb.
rows: Could I stop halfway through it?
Can something come straight after it?
Does the sentence name who did it?

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *She is owning three flats.* / *She owns three flats.*
items.why: Owning is a state. There is no middle of owning to be in.

items.prompt: Why is *The strike was occurred in April* wrong?
items.answer: *Occur* cannot take an object, so it cannot be turned round. Write *The strike occurred in April.*
items.why: Nothing is done to the strike. The strike is the whole event.

terms_introduced.gloss: a verb that describes a state, not an action

related_articles.reason: the form these verbs are refusing, built in full
the wider choice between the plain form and the *-ing* form
verbs made of two or three words, such as *carry out* and *result in*
the clause shapes an object sits in

intents: know whether a verb needs something after it

article_json.one_line: This is the form for what does not depend on today, so you can state a fact, a habit, a state or a timetable.
article_json.short_answer: Use the base form. Add *-s* for *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing. *The depot opens at seven.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say what is generally true?

body.text: This form says: that is how things are
Use it for anything that does not depend on today. Facts, habits, rules, states and timetables all sit here. Nothing in the form says the event is going on at this minute.
So it is the ordinary form for explaining how a system works, and the ordinary form for describing a chart or a process.
Build it from the base form, and add *-s* for one thing

body.caption: Only the *he* row changes. Every other row is the base form.
body.form_line: the base form, plus *-s* for *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing

rows.note: The only row that changes, and the *-s* moves onto *does*.

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats the helping verb and stops.
Add *do* to a positive sentence when you are contradicting somebody.
rows: somebody has just said it does not
to insist that it is true

examples.text: The Verdon depot paints the bridge railings every third summer.
examples.gloss: It happens on a three-year cycle.

examples.text: The surveyor writes a short note after each visit.
examples.gloss: That is part of the job every time.

examples.text: We don't paint over the numbers on the posts.
examples.gloss: The numbers have to stay readable.

examples.text: Does he write the summary himself?
examples.gloss: The question is who does that piece of work.

notes: The *-s* moves onto *does* in a negative or a question. Never *he doesn't paints*.
There is no positive short form here. *I'm paint* and *he's paint* are not English.
Spelling of the *-s* ending is set out in [th_spelling_and_sound_of_endings].

body.text: The five jobs this one form does

body.caption: Five different meanings, and one form covers all of them.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: a fact that does not change
Coastal towns flood more often than inland ones.
something you do again and again
She cycles to the depot twice a week.
a situation that is set to last
My brother works for a housing charity.
a state rather than an action
The trust owns four listed buildings.
The last ferry leaves at eleven.
footnotes: The last row is about tomorrow, not about every day. The form does not care.

body.lead_in: One example for each row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: the job the form is doing

items.text: Older buildings lose heat through the roof first.
items.gloss: That is true of older buildings in general.

items.text: I check the water meter on the first of the month.
items.gloss: It is a habit, once a month.

items.text: The charity runs three shops in the town.
items.gloss: That is the situation, and it is not about to change.

items.text: The new pass costs less than a weekly ticket.
items.gloss: That is the price.

items.text: The course starts on the second Monday in October.
items.gloss: That is the date in the timetable.

body.so_what: Five different meanings came out in the same shape, and no time word was needed for three of them.

body.text: Use the present simple when the sentence is about how things are, not about what is going on at this moment.

body.lead_in: None of these is happening at the moment of speaking.

items.text: Night buses run every forty minutes at weekends.
items.gloss: That is the pattern, whether one is running now or not.

items.text: My flat faces the railway, so mornings are noisy.
items.gloss: That is where the windows point.

items.text: The trust employs eleven people across the two sites.
items.gloss: That is the size of the staff.

body.so_what: Each one is true today, was true last month, and says nothing about this minute.

body.text: Where the *-s* goes missing, and where it goes twice

body.wrong: The scheme costs very little and help two hundred families.
body.right: The scheme costs very little and helps two hundred families.
body.why_it_happens: You put the *-s* on the first verb and then move on. By the time the second verb arrives, the subject is several words behind and out of mind.
body.smallest_fix: Check every verb in the sentence, not only the one nearest the subject.

body.wrong: Does the council knows about the leak?
body.right: Does the council know about the leak?
body.why_it_happens: The subject is one thing, so the *-s* feels compulsory. *Does* has already taken it, and English marks it in one place only.
body.smallest_fix: After *do*, *does* or *did*, go back to the base form.

body.wrong: The new bins collects more waste than the old ones.
body.right: The new bins collect more waste than the old ones.
body.why_it_happens: An *-s* on the noun and an *-s* on the verb look as though they belong together. They are opposites: the *-s* on the verb means one, and on the noun it means more than one.
body.smallest_fix: Count the subject. More than one means no *-s* on the verb.

body.heard: The present simple is the tense for things you do every day.
body.truth: Habits are one of its five jobs. It also carries facts, states, rules and timetables. *The last ferry leaves at eleven* is about tomorrow evening, not about every day of your life.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the sentence is about how things are rather than what is under way now. If it is, this is the form, however often the thing happens.

body.mechanism: Chinese verbs keep one shape whatever the subject is, and who is doing the action is shown by the words in front of the verb.
body.wrong: My neighbour repair bicycles at the weekend.
body.right: My neighbour repairs bicycles at the weekend.
body.fix: Add *-s* whenever the subject is *he*, *she*, *it* or a single thing.

body.headline: Base form everywhere, plus *-s* for one thing.

articles.title: Saying what is going on around now

article_json.one_line: This is the form for something under way, so you can say what is happening now and what is only temporary.
article_json.short_answer: Use *am*, *is* or *are* with the *-ing* form. *The crew is painting the bridge this week.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something is going on at the moment?

body.text: This form says: it has started and it has not finished
Use it when the event has a middle and you are standing in it. Nothing in the form says the job will be finished, so it is the natural way to talk about a temporary arrangement.
Around now counts as well as right now. *House prices are rising* is true this year, even though nothing is going up as you read it.
Build it from *be* and the *-ing* form

body.caption: Only *be* changes. The *-ing* form never moves.
body.form_line: *am*, *is* or *are* plus the *-ing* form of the main verb

rows.note: Only one short form here. *Amn't* is not standard English.

sub_tables.caption: A positive short answer never uses a short form.
*He's* has two expansions, and the next word tells you which.

examples.text: They're painting the Verdon bridge this week.
examples.gloss: The work started and it is not done yet.

examples.text: She is writing the Norland report at the moment.
examples.gloss: That is the job in front of her today.

examples.text: We aren't painting the west span until the funding lands.
examples.gloss: That part of the work is on hold.

examples.text: Is he writing the summary or the covering note?
examples.gloss: The question is which piece he has in hand.

notes: *I'm not* is the only short form for the *I* row. The *am* contracts, never the *not*.
Never *Yes, I'm.* A short answer cannot end on a short form.
The negative question for *I* is *Aren't I painting?*, which is irregular and standard.

body.caption: The event started before now and has not reached its end.

spec.caption: A bar across now, with no end marked

body.text: The four jobs this form does

body.caption: Four meanings, and only the first is about this minute.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: it is going on right now
The lift is stuck between floors.
I am covering the late shift this month.
it is a change still under way
Rents in the old quarter are climbing again.
it is fixed in a diary
We are meeting the contractor on Thursday.
footnotes: The fourth row is about the future. The full set of future forms is in [th_the_futures].

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: the job the form is doing

items.text: The alarm is going off again in the stairwell.
items.gloss: You can hear it as you speak.

items.text: She is staying with her sister until the flat is ready.
items.gloss: It is an arrangement with an end in sight.

items.text: Fewer households are heating with gas each winter.
items.gloss: The pattern is shifting and has not settled.

items.text: I am seeing the housing officer on Friday morning.
items.gloss: The appointment is already made.

body.so_what: Only the first one is happening at this minute, and all four use the same form.

body.text: Use *be* plus the *-ing* form when the event has a middle and you are inside it, or when the situation has an end in sight.

body.lead_in: Each of these has an end the speaker can see coming.

items.text: The library is running reduced hours during the repairs.
items.gloss: It will go back to normal when the work ends.

items.text: I'm cycling in while the bus route is closed.
items.gloss: It is not how I normally travel.

items.text: Two of the wards are taking patients from the north site.
items.gloss: It is an arrangement for the moment.

body.so_what: In every one of them, things will go back to how they were.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The number of cyclists rising every year since the lane opened.
body.right: The number of cyclists is rising every year since the lane opened.
body.why_it_happens: The *-ing* form looks like a verb and feels like enough. On its own it carries no time, so the group of words is not yet a sentence.
body.smallest_fix: Put *is* or *are* in front of the *-ing* form.

body.wrong: I am wanting a room away from the road.
body.right: I want a room away from the road.
body.why_it_happens: The want is real at this minute, and this is the form for this minute. Wanting is a state, and a state has no middle to stand in.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the helping verb and the *-ing*: *I want*.

body.wrong: The council is repair the footbridge this month.
body.right: The council is repairing the footbridge this month.
body.why_it_happens: *Is* already feels like the verb of the sentence, so the second word is left in its dictionary shape. After *be*, the main verb always takes *-ing*.
body.smallest_fix: Add *-ing* to the word after *am*, *is* or *are*.

body.label: Two uses that look like errors and are not

items.text: *Always* with this form is a complaint, not a habit.
items.example: The upstairs tap is always dripping.

items.text: A state verb takes this form when it names something you are doing.
items.example: The technician is testing how the sample tastes.

body.heard: The present continuous means it is happening at this exact moment.
body.truth: Right now is one of its four jobs. *Rents are climbing again* is not happening this second, and *We are meeting the contractor on Thursday* has not happened at all yet.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the situation is temporary rather than whether it is happening this second. Keep *now* as the commonest case of temporary, not as the rule.

article_json.one_line: This lets you choose between two present forms that are both correct, so the sentence says whether the situation lasts.
article_json.short_answer: Ask whether it lasts. Permanent or repeated, use *she teaches*. Temporary or still moving, use *she is teaching*.

body.text: Both are correct, and they say different things
*He lectures at the college* and *He is lecturing at the college* are both good English. Neither is more advanced than the other. A reader hears a real difference between them.
So the choice is not about the form. It is about whether the situation is set to last, or has an end somewhere in view.
Is this permanent, or is there an end in sight?

body.question: Does this situation last, or does it have an end in sight?

options.label: present simple
options.use_it_when: It lasts, it repeats, or it is a fact, a rule, a state or a timetable.
options.example: The market opens at six on Saturdays.

options.label: present continuous
options.use_it_when: It is temporary, it is under way at the moment, or it is a change that has not settled.
options.example: The market is opening later while the road is dug up.

body.deciding_factor: Permanent or repeated, use the plain form. Temporary or still moving, use *be* plus the *-ing* form.
body.trap: You were told that the *-ing* form means now, so anything true at this minute seems to need it. Plenty of things are true now without being under way now.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The choice pays hardest in Speaking Part 1, where *I usually cycle in* and *I am cycling more at the moment* answer two different questions.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Would this still be true in six months?

branches.answer: No — you are stating how things stand

verdict.example: Rents in the north of the town are lower.
verdict.why: You are reporting a fact, not a movement.

body.text: Use the present simple for what lasts. Use the present continuous for what is temporary or still moving.

body.lead_in: No time expression in any of these. The verb is doing the work alone.

items.gloss: Something is wrong with it at the moment.

body.so_what: Nothing in the words around the verb decided these. The verb itself carried the meaning.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: At the moment I am preferring the earlier train.
body.right: At the moment I prefer the earlier train.
body.why_it_happens: *At the moment* looks like a signal for the *-ing* form, so it drags the verb with it. Preferring is a state, and a state stays in the plain form even when the time word says now.
body.smallest_fix: Leave the time words alone and put the state verb in the plain form.

body.wrong: Since the charge came in, traffic in the centre falls steadily.
body.right: Since the charge came in, traffic in the centre is falling steadily.
body.why_it_happens: A fall in traffic sounds like a fact, and facts take the plain form. This one is a movement that has not stopped, and a movement takes the *-ing* form.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether the number has settled. If it is still moving, use *is* plus *-ing*.

body.heard: Present continuous is for now, and present simple is for every day.
body.truth: It breaks in both directions. *Rents are climbing again* is not happening this second, and *The ferry leaves at six* is about one departure tomorrow rather than every day.
body.what_to_do: Swap the pair for permanent against temporary. Treat right now as the commonest kind of temporary, which is why the old rule works often enough to survive.

body.text: This form says: it happened, and it is over
Use it when the event sits inside a stretch of time that has closed. The stretch is often named, and often just understood by both of you.
It is the spine of any story. One finished event after another, in the order they happened, is what a listener expects to hear.
One form for every subject, and *did* for the rest

rows.note: No *-s* anywhere. The past simple has no person endings.

body.text: The stretch of time is closed, however recent it is
Use the past simple when the stretch of time you have in mind is over, whether that stretch ended a decade ago or a minute ago.

body.lead_in: The time words move from very recent to very distant. The verb does not care.

items.text: The lights went out about ten seconds ago.
items.gloss: It has just happened, and it is over.

items.text: The council approved the parking scheme last March.
items.gloss: The decision was taken then.

items.text: Both mills closed before my grandmother was born.
items.gloss: They shut a very long time ago.

items.text: I dropped the keys somewhere between the gate and the door.
items.gloss: It happened on the walk in.

body.so_what: Ten seconds and a hundred years took the same form, because in both the stretch of time has closed.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The inspector didn't wrote anything in the log.
body.right: The inspector didn't write anything in the log.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about the past, so the past form of the verb feels required. *Did* has already carried the past, and English carries it once.
body.smallest_fix: After *did* or *didn't*, use the base form: *write*, *paint*, *go*.

body.wrong: Nobody knowed about the second entrance.
body.right: Nobody knew about the second entrance.
body.why_it_happens: Adding *-ed* is the rule, and it works for most verbs. A few hundred common verbs change shape instead, and they are the ones you use most often.
body.smallest_fix: Look the verb up in [th_irregular_verbs] once, and learn it in its group.

body.wrong: The two engineers was still on site at eight.
body.right: The two engineers were still on site at eight.
body.why_it_happens: *Was* is the form you hear most, so it comes first. *Be* is the only verb left with a past ending, and it needs *were* for more than one.
body.smallest_fix: Count the subject. More than one takes *were*.

body.heard: The past simple is for things that happened a long time ago.
also_known_as: past simple means finished long ago
body.truth: Distance has nothing to do with it. *The lights went out ten seconds ago* is past simple. What decides it is that the stretch of time has closed, not how far away it is.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the stretch of time is over. If it is over, use the past simple, even if it closed a minute ago.

body.mechanism: Spanish marks the past on the end of the verb and changes that ending for each person, so a separate helping verb is not needed for a question.
body.wrong: Wrote you the covering note?
body.right: Did you write the covering note?
body.fix: Build a past question with *did* plus the base form, and leave the main verb alone.

article_json.one_line: This is the form for something already under way at a past moment, so a shorter event can cut across it.
article_json.short_answer: Use *was* or *were* with the *-ing* form. *We were painting the hall when the pipe burst.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say what was already going on when something else happened?

body.text: This form paints the scene. It does not move the story on
Something was already running when the moment you care about arrived. That is the whole job. The shorter event that lands in the middle of it takes the past simple.
So the two forms work as a pair. One is the picture, and the other is the thing that happens in front of it.
Build it from *was* or *were* and the *-ing* form

body.caption: Only *be* changes, and it changes in one place: *was* against *were*.
body.form_line: *was* or *were* plus the *-ing* form of the main verb

rows: While I was waiting, the power went out.

notes: *Was* goes with *I*, *he*, *she* and *it*. *Were* goes with *you*, *we* and *they*.
A state verb stays in the past simple here as well: *I knew*, never *I was knowing*.

body.text: Was it the whole event, or the background to one?

body.question: Is this the event itself, or the situation the event landed in?

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: The event is complete and it moves the story on to the next thing.
options.example: The surveyor arrived at nine and left before lunch.

options.label: past continuous
options.use_it_when: The situation was already running, and you are setting the scene rather than moving it on.
options.example: The surveyor was measuring the roof when the rain started.

a.text: When the manager arrived, the crew left.
a.means: The crew went after she got there, and probably because she did.

b.text: When the manager arrived, the crew were leaving.
b.means: They were already on their way out when she walked in.

a.text: I read the tenancy agreement on the train.
a.means: I got to the end of it before I arrived.

b.text: I was reading the tenancy agreement on the train.
b.means: That is what I had in my hands. It says nothing about finishing.

a.text: The kettle boiled and the fuse went.
a.means: The kettle finished boiling, and then the fuse blew.

b.text: The kettle was boiling and the fuse went.
b.means: The kettle was still going when the fuse blew.

a.text: She cooked while I laid the table.
a.means: Two finished jobs, one after the other or side by side.

b.text: She was cooking while I laid the table.
b.means: The cooking was the longer job, running underneath mine.

body.deciding_factor: Short, finished and moving the story on, use the past simple. Longer, unfinished and setting the scene, use *was* plus *-ing*.
body.trap: The *-ing* form feels more descriptive, so it looks like the better choice for a story. Put a whole story in it and nothing ever happens, because the form never finishes anything.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The pair pays hardest in Speaking Part 2, where a two-minute story needs a scene as well as a sequence of events.

body.text: Use the past continuous for the situation that was already running. Use the past simple for the event that landed inside it.

body.lead_in: Each sentence has one of each. The longer thing takes the *-ing* form.

items.text: I was locking up when the alarm panel started beeping.
items.gloss: The locking up had begun; the beeping cut across it.

items.text: While the ward was moving beds, two ambulances arrived.
items.gloss: The move was under way when they turned up.

items.text: The bus was pulling away as she reached the stop.
items.gloss: She missed it by a few seconds.

body.so_what: In each one, the *-ing* form is the longer thing and the plain past form is the moment.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Last summer I was travelling to Marlow, I was visiting the museum and I was buying a ticket.
body.right: Last summer I travelled to Marlow, visited the museum and bought a ticket.
body.why_it_happens: The *-ing* form sounds richer, so it gets used for everything. Nothing in it ever finishes, so the story stops moving and the listener waits for the point.
body.smallest_fix: Keep the *-ing* form for the scene. Put every event that moves the story on in the past simple.

body.wrong: The volunteers was clearing the towpath all morning.
body.right: The volunteers were clearing the towpath all morning.
body.why_it_happens: *Was* is the commoner word, so it arrives first. This is the one past form left in English that still changes for the subject.
body.smallest_fix: Count the subject. More than one takes *were*.

body.wrong: I was knowing the answer before she finished the question.
body.right: I knew the answer before she finished the question.
body.why_it_happens: The knowing lasted through the moment, and this is the form for things that last through a moment. Knowing is a state, so there is no middle of it to stand in.
body.smallest_fix: Put the state verb in the past simple: *I knew*, *I wanted*, *I owned*.

body.heard: *While* always takes the past continuous and *when* always takes the past simple.
body.truth: It is a useful habit, not a rule. *While I was waiting* and *when the power went out* are the common shapes, but *While she checked the meter, I held the torch* is correct, and so is *When I was living in Norland, rents were lower*.
body.what_to_do: Choose the form by asking which event is the longer one. Then put *when* or *while* in front of whichever clause needs it.

body.headline: The long thing gets *-ing*. The moment gets the plain past.

articles.title: Talking about what you used to do

article_json.also_called: *Used to*, *would* and the past simple for past habits
article_json.one_line: This lets you pick between three ways of talking about the past, so the sentence says whether things have changed.
article_json.short_answer: Use *used to* when the point is that it is not true now. *Would* works for repeated actions only, never for states.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something was true then and is not true now?

body.text: Three ways to talk about the past, and they are not the same
*We used to live above the shop*, *We lived above the shop* and *Every summer we would repaint the boat* are all correct. What separates them is whether you are pointing at a change.
There is also a fourth structure that looks identical and means something else entirely. *I am used to working nights* is about now, not about the past.
Is it a state, a repeated action, or one event?

body.question: Was this a state, a repeated action, or a single event?

options.label: *used to* + base form
options.use_it_when: It was true then and is not true now, and that change is the point. It works for states and for actions.
options.example: The station used to have a waiting room.

options.label: *would* + base form
options.use_it_when: It is a repeated action inside a past time you have already set up. Never use it for a state.
options.example: Every August the yard would close for two weeks.

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: It is one finished event, or a habit where you are making no claim about now.
options.example: We lived above the shop for six years.

a.text: I used to walk to the depot.
a.means: I do not walk there any more, and that change is the news.

b.means: That is what I did then. Nothing is claimed about now.

a.text: Every winter the pond used to freeze.
a.means: It froze then and it does not any more.

b.text: Every winter the pond would freeze.
b.means: You are remembering those winters from inside the story.

a.text: He used to have a motorbike.
a.means: He owned one then and he does not now.

b.means: He owned one at the time you are talking about.

a.means: I worked nights then and I do not now.

b.text: I am used to working nights.
b.means: I work nights now and it feels normal to me.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: used to work / am used to working

body.deciding_factor: *Used to* for anything that was true then and is not now. *Would* for repeated actions only, once the past time is already set.
body.trap: *Used to* and *would* are taught as swappable, so *would* gets used for states. *She would be shy* is grammatical and means something completely different.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere, and *used to* is one of the strongest Speaking Part 3 moves for saying how things have changed.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Is it a state, such as having, being, knowing or living somewhere?

verdict.example: The yard used to belong to the railway.
verdict.why: *Would* cannot carry a state. It turns the sentence into something else.

steps.ask: Is the point that it does not happen any more?

verdict.example: The trust used to run a bus to the coast.
verdict.why: *Used to* carries the contrast with now on its own, with no extra words.

steps.ask: Have you already told the reader which past time you mean?

branches.answer: Yes, and it happened again and again

verdict.example: Every August the yard would close for two weeks.
verdict.why: *Would* leans on a past time frame that is already in place.

verdict.example: The yard closed for two weeks that August.
verdict.why: One finished event in closed time is what the past simple is for.

body.text: The first question does most of the work. States are where *would* goes wrong, and states are common, because having, being and living somewhere are all states.
The four shapes, side by side

body.caption: Two take the base form. The last two take the *-ing* form.

it feels normal to me now
I am becoming accustomed to it
footnotes: The *to* in the last two rows is a small placing word, which is why an *-ing* form follows it.
*Used to* has no present form. For a present habit use the present simple with *usually*.

items.gloss: It does not open on Sundays any more.

body.so_what: The first two are about the past. The last two are about how something feels now.

body.text: Use *used to* whenever the sentence says that something was true then and is not true now. Use *would* for repeated actions only.

body.lead_in: Every one of these is a state, so *would* is unavailable in all of them.

items.text: The building used to belong to the water company.
items.gloss: Somebody else owns it now.

items.text: There used to be a chemist on the corner.
items.gloss: It has gone.

items.text: I used to know everybody on the street.
items.gloss: Most of them have moved away.

body.so_what: Belonging, being there and knowing people are all states, and none of them is something you repeatedly did.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I didn't used to cycle in the winter.
body.right: I didn't use to cycle in the winter.
body.why_it_happens: *Used to* is learned as one block, so the *d* travels with it everywhere. *Did* has already taken the past, so what follows goes back to the base form.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *d* after *did* and *didn't*: *Did you use to…?*

body.wrong: She would be very shy as a child.
body.right: She used to be very shy as a child.
body.why_it_happens: *Would* and *used to* look interchangeable, so the swap seems free. *Would* cannot carry a state, and the sentence turns into a guess about what she is like.
body.smallest_fix: If the verb names a state, use *used to* or the past simple.

body.wrong: I am used to live near the station before the move.
body.right: I used to live near the station before the move.
body.why_it_happens: The two structures share four letters and sound almost the same. One is about the past and takes the base form; the other is about now and takes the *-ing* form.
body.smallest_fix: For the past, drop *am* and keep the base form: *I used to live*.

body.heard: *Used to* and *would* mean the same thing, so you can use whichever sounds better.
also_known_as: would is the more advanced used to
body.truth: They overlap for repeated actions and nowhere else. *Would* cannot carry a state, so *I would have a motorbike* does not mean that you owned one. It reads as a guess about a situation that is not real.
body.what_to_do: Check what the verb names. A state takes *used to* or the past simple. A repeated action takes any of the three, and *would* needs the past time already set up.

body.headline: *Used to* for a change. *Would* for actions only.

articles.title: The idea behind every *have* plus third form

article_json.one_line: This is the one idea behind four of the twelve tenses, so you can learn them as a single thing instead of four.
article_json.short_answer: *Have* plus the third form stands at one point and looks back at an earlier one. Move the *have* and you move the standing point.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What do all the *have* forms have in common?

body.text: Every perfect form has two points in it, not one
A plain past form gives you one point: it happened. A perfect form gives you two. There is the point where the thing happened, and the point you are standing at when you mention it.
That is why these forms feel harder. You are not choosing when something happened. You are choosing where to stand while you talk about it.
Move the *have*, and you move where you stand

body.caption: The third form never moves. Only the word in front of it changes.
rows: The trust has repaired the west span.
at a past moment, looking back
By April the trust had repaired it.
at a future moment, looking back
By June the trust will have repaired it.
footnotes: The fourth member of the family adds *been* and an *-ing* form, and measures how long: *has been repairing*.

body.lead_in: One event, three standing points. Only the word in front of *repaired* changes.

items.text: The council has repaired both footbridges.
items.gloss: They are usable now. That is the situation today.

items.text: By the inspection the council had repaired both footbridges.
items.gloss: The work was already finished when the inspector came.

items.text: By September the council will have repaired both footbridges.
items.gloss: The work will be behind them by then.

items.text: They've repaired the handrail twice this winter.
items.gloss: It keeps breaking, and the winter is not over.

body.so_what: The repair happened once. What moved is the moment from which you are looking at it.

body.caption: An arrow from the event to the point you are standing at.

body.text: The second word is the third form, and it never changes
Whatever the first word is, the word behind it is always the third form of the main verb. For a regular verb that looks exactly like the past form. For an irregular verb it does not.
Put *have*, *has*, *had* or *will have* in front, and the third form of the main verb behind. The main verb takes no other shape.

body.lead_in: Two verbs, one regular and one irregular, in the same three shapes.

items.text: The crew has painted the whole span.
items.gloss: The span is painted now.

items.text: The crew has written up the inspection notes.
items.gloss: The notes exist and are ready to read.

items.text: By Friday they had painted every railing on the bridge.
items.gloss: That job was finished before Friday.

items.text: They'd written to the residents before the work started.
items.gloss: The letters went out first.

body.so_what: *Painted* looks the same as the past form and *written* does not. The grammar is identical in both.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The panel has wrote to every household on the estate.
body.right: The panel has written to every household on the estate.
body.why_it_happens: With a regular verb the past form and the third form are the same word, so the two never need telling apart. With an irregular verb they are different, and the past form comes to hand first.
body.smallest_fix: After *have*, *has*, *had* or *will have*, use the third form: *written*, *taken*, *gone*.

body.wrong: The surveyor has gone to the site twice this month, so she knows it well.
body.right: The surveyor has been to the site twice this month, so she knows it well.
body.why_it_happens: *Gone* is the ordinary third form of *go*, so it looks like the right choice. *Has gone* means the person is still away; *has been* means they went and came back.
body.smallest_fix: Use *been* when the person has returned, and *gone* when they have not.

body.wrong: The tenants would of noticed a leak that size.
body.right: The tenants would have noticed a leak that size.
body.why_it_happens: *Would have* is squeezed to *would've* in speech, and that sounds exactly like *would of*. There is no verb *of*, so the word is always *have*.
body.smallest_fix: Write *have* every time. The same goes for *should have* and *could have*.

body.label: Two things that look like this family and are not

items.text: *Have got* means *have*. It is not a perfect form at all.
items.example: They've got two more sites to inspect.

items.text: *'d* stands for *had* in front of a third form and for *would* in front of a base form.
items.example: They'd painted it. They'd paint it.

body.heard: The present perfect is one of the past tenses.
also_known_as: have done is a past tense
the perfect tenses are past tenses
body.truth: *Has repaired* is built on *has*, which is a present form. That is why the sentence is about how things stand now. A perfect form always reports from where you are standing, and *has* puts you at now.
body.what_to_do: Read the first word rather than the second. *Has* means you are standing at now, *had* at a past moment, and *will have* at a future one.

body.headline: The first word says where you stand. The second never moves.

articles.title: Saying that something before now still matters

article_json.one_line: This is the form for something that happened earlier and still counts today, so the sentence stays about now.
article_json.short_answer: Use *have* or *has* with the third form. *The ward has closed to visitors.* Something happened, and it matters now.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something happened and it still matters?

body.text: This form keeps the sentence about now
The event is behind you. The point of the sentence is in front of you. That is what this form buys: something happened, and here is where it leaves us.
So it is the form for reporting a position rather than telling a story. Nothing in it says when, and that is deliberate.
Build it from *have* or *has* and the third form

body.caption: Only *have* changes, and only in the *he* row. The third form never moves.
body.form_line: *have* or *has* plus the third form of the main verb

rows.note: The only row where the helping verb changes.

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats the helping verb and stops there.
The word after *have* is the third form, not the past form.
Two ways to shorten the negative, and both are correct.

examples.text: The contractors have painted the Verdon river bridge.
examples.gloss: The bridge is painted, and that is where things stand.

examples.text: The inspector has written to both landlords.
examples.gloss: The letters are with them now.

examples.text: We haven't painted the lamp posts yet.
examples.gloss: That part of the job is still waiting.

examples.text: Has she written up the meter readings?
examples.gloss: The question is whether they are recorded.

notes: *He's painted* is *he has painted*. The third form behind it is the clue.
Never *Yes, I've.* A short answer cannot end on a short form.
The *'ve not* and *'s not* negatives are commoner in British English than in American English. Both are correct everywhere.

body.caption: Four contexts, and in all four the answer to *when* is not the point.

footnotes: In every row the reader can still ask *when?* and be told that it does not matter.

items.text: The water company has cut off the supply to the block.
items.gloss: There is no water in the taps at the moment.

items.text: I have never worked a night shift before.
items.gloss: In my whole working life it has not happened.

items.text: The charity has run the food bank since the mill closed.
items.gloss: It started then and it is still running it.

items.text: Two of the tutors have already handed in their notice.
items.gloss: The department is going to be short.

body.so_what: Not one of those sentences tells you the date, and not one of them needs to.

body.caption: The event sits back there; the arrow lands on now.

spec.caption: Back there, but pointing at today

body.text: Use the present perfect when the point of the sentence is where things stand now, or when the stretch of time is still open.

body.lead_in: No time expression in any of these. The verb is carrying the meaning alone.

items.text: The lift has broken down again.
items.gloss: It is out of order, and that is the problem.

items.text: The committee has agreed the new route.
items.gloss: The route is settled. That is where things stand.

items.text: Two of the surveyors have resigned.
items.gloss: They are gone, and the team is two people short.

body.so_what: Each one reports a position rather than an event, which is why no date is needed.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Since the new timetable came in, journey times improved.
body.right: Since the new timetable came in, journey times have improved.
body.why_it_happens: *Since* points backwards, so a past form feels like the natural partner. *Since* opens a stretch that runs up to today, and the verb inside it has to stay open too.
body.smallest_fix: Change *improved* to *have improved*. The stretch from the timetable change is still running.

body.wrong: The office has took on two more apprentices.
body.right: The office has taken on two more apprentices.
body.why_it_happens: For a regular verb the past form and the third form are the same word, so the two never need separating. *Take* separates them, and the past form is the one you say more often.
body.smallest_fix: After *have* or *has*, use the third form: *taken*, *written*, *gone*.

body.wrong: The two clinics has moved to the new health centre.
body.right: The two clinics have moved to the new health centre.
body.why_it_happens: The word nearest the verb is a single building, so *has* sounds right. The subject is the two clinics, and the helping verb matches the subject.
body.smallest_fix: Find the subject, count it, and pick *have* or *has* from that.

body.label: Three cases where this looks broken and is not

items.text: After *this is the first time*, English uses this form even though the frame is present.
items.example: This is the first time the ward has closed to visitors.

items.text: *Since* can give a reason rather than a start point, and then no perfect form is needed.
items.example: Since the ward is short-staffed, visiting hours are limited.

items.text: *Have got* means *have*. It is not a perfect form at all.
items.example: I've got the spare keys in my bag.

also_known_as: if you see since, use the perfect
body.truth: It holds when *since* marks a start point. *Since* has a second job: it can mean *because*, as in *Since the ward is short-staffed, visiting hours are limited*, and then the verb is whatever the sentence needs.
body.what_to_do: Ask what *since* is doing. Marking a start point takes *have* plus the third form. Giving a reason takes no special form at all.

body.headline: *Have* or *has*, then the third form. It happened; it counts now.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *He has forgot the code.* / *He has forgotten the code.*
items.why: After *has*, the verb takes its third form, and for *forget* that is *forgotten*.

items.prompt: Why does *Since April the queue got longer* need changing?
items.answer: *Since April* is still running, so the verb stays open: *has got longer*.
items.why: A stretch that reaches today needs a verb that reaches today.

articles.title: Saying how long something has been going on

article_json.one_line: This is the form for measuring how long an activity has run up to now, so the length becomes the point.
article_json.short_answer: Use *have been* or *has been* with the *-ing* form. *The crew has been painting since April.* The length is the point.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say how long something has been going on?

body.text: This form measures the activity, not the result
Something has been running for a while and it reaches up to now. The sentence is about the running of it, so it often explains why things look the way they do.
It does not promise that the activity is finished, and it does not promise that it has stopped. It only tells you how long it went on.
Build it from *have been* and the *-ing* form

body.caption: Only *have* changes. *Been* and the *-ing* form never move.
body.form_line: *have been* or *has been* plus the *-ing* form of the main verb

rows.note: The only row where the helping verb changes.

sub_tables.caption: The short answer drops everything except the helping verb.
*How long* and this form are a standing partnership.
rows: How long have you been painting?
How long has she been writing it?

examples.text: The contractors have been painting the bridge since April.
examples.gloss: The job started in April and it is still going.

examples.text: She's been writing the Ashfield chapter all morning.
examples.gloss: That is what she has been doing since she sat down.

examples.text: The team has not been painting in this weather.
examples.gloss: Work has been held up by the rain.

examples.text: Have they been writing to residents about the closure?
examples.gloss: The question is whether letters have been going out.

notes: *He's been painting* is *he has been painting*. The *been* is what tells you.
A state verb has no form here. Write *I have known her for years*, never *I have been knowing her*.
*How long* pulls this form more strongly than any other words in English.

spec.caption: The length of the bar is the point

body.text: The two jobs this form does

body.caption: Two meanings, and the second one is the reason nobody teaches this form well.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: how long it has run, and it is still running
The pump has been running since Tuesday.
why things look the way they do now
You can tell he has been decorating.
footnotes: In the second row the activity has usually stopped. What is left behind is the evidence.

body.lead_in: The first two measure the length. The last two explain what you can see.

items.text: The council has been consulting residents since the spring.
items.gloss: The consultation started then and is not over.

items.text: I've been waiting at this stop for forty minutes.
items.gloss: The wait started forty minutes ago and it goes on.

items.text: Her eyes are red because she has been staring at figures.
items.gloss: That is what has made her eyes sore.

items.text: The corridor smells of paint. Somebody has been decorating.
items.gloss: The smell is the evidence of the work.

body.so_what: In the last two the work has stopped, and the sentence is still correct.

body.text: Use *have been* plus the *-ing* form when the length of an activity is the point, or when its traces explain the present situation.

body.lead_in: Each one answers the question *how long*, with a different kind of answer.

items.text: The clinic has been running Saturday sessions for a year.
items.gloss: They started a year ago and they are still on.

items.text: We've been sharing an office since the refit started.
items.gloss: The sharing began with the refit and continues.

items.text: Fares have been rising steadily since the fuel levy.
items.gloss: The rise began then and has not stopped.

body.so_what: Each one names a starting point, and the stretch from it reaches today.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I have been reading four chapters this morning.
body.right: I have read four chapters this morning.
body.why_it_happens: The reading went on all morning, so the form for a long activity looks right. A counted amount is a finished result, and a finished result needs the plain third form.
body.smallest_fix: Drop *been* and the *-ing* whenever the sentence gives a number.

body.wrong: They have been knowing each other since college.
body.right: They have known each other since college.
body.why_it_happens: The knowing has lasted for years, and this is the form for something that lasts. Knowing is a state, and a state cannot be shown in the middle of happening.
body.smallest_fix: Use *have* plus the third form: *have known*, *have owned*, *have believed*.

body.wrong: The pump has running since Tuesday without a break.
body.right: The pump has been running since Tuesday without a break.
body.why_it_happens: *Has running* sounds close enough to be missed, especially in speech where *been* is unstressed. The form needs all three words, in that order.
body.smallest_fix: Put *been* between the helping verb and the *-ing* form.

body.heard: The present perfect continuous means the activity is still going on.
also_known_as: have been doing means it has not stopped
body.truth: It often is still going on, and it does not have to be. *Somebody has been decorating* is normally said about a job that finished an hour ago, because the point is the smell of paint rather than the painting.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the length or the traces of the activity are the point. If they are, this form is right, whether the activity has stopped or not.

body.headline: *Have been* plus *-ing*. The length is the message.
